title: Touchscreen MacBook Pro rumours: Release date, OLED, specs and latest leaks
content:
Macworld





The touchscreen MacBook Pro has been the subject of speculation ever since Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman first reported in 2023 that Apple was exploring the idea. At the time, the claim seemed hard to believe given Apple’s long-standing opposition to touchscreen laptops. Three years later, however, the rumours are becoming increasingly difficult to dismiss.
Multiple reports suggest Apple has overcome the technical and design challenges that previously stood in the way. If they’re accurate, the first touchscreen MacBook Pro will arrive as part of one of the biggest redesigns in the laptop’s history, combining a new chassis with Apple’s first OLED MacBook display and potentially even an iPhone-style Dynamic Island camera cutout.
The timing would be fitting. The MacBook Pro celebrates its 20th anniversary in 2026, and Apple could mark the milestone with a feature many believed would never come to the Mac. Touchscreen support would also help further differentiate the MacBook Pro from the MacBook Air and the budget-friendly MacBook Neo.
There are still questions over pricing. OLED panels and ongoing supply-chain pressures are expected to make the new models more expensive than today’s MacBook Pro. Apple is also expected to keep touchscreen technology exclusive to its premium laptops initially, with no indication that it will come to the MacBook Air or MacBook Neo in the first generation. Read on for a complete roundup of the latest touchscreen MacBook Pro rumours, including what the most reliable sources are saying, how credible each report is, and what we think Apple is likely to announce and when.


Touchscreen MacBook Pro release date: When will it launch?
October 28, 2026 confirmed 
On October 19, Apple announced a media event, dubbed “Pro and Tell” on October 28, 2026. This is expected to be the introduction of new Macs, including the touchscreen MacBook Pro.


Can’t wait to pro and tell next week. pic.twitter.com/3wUkxwq35i
— Greg Joswiak (@gregjoz) October 19, 2026





Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported on October 8 that Apple plans to announce its first touchscreen MacBook on October 27. The launch will reportedly include an online video presentation and an in-person component for the press on October 28. In his Power On podcast, Gurman said the laptop will start shipping on November 6.
Earlier reports offered a broader launch window and raised the possibility of delays. Speaking in a Power On podcast on October 1, Gurman said he expected the touchscreen MacBook announcement as early as October, potentially slipping to November. The laptops are reportedly being tested with macOS 27.2.
In September 2026, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman included the touchscreen MacBooks in a list of products that will ship in late 2026/early 2027.
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman and analyst Ming-Chi Kuo both initially predicted a late 2026 debut, with an October announcement fitting Apple’s traditional MacBook Pro release schedule while also coinciding with the 20th anniversary of the MacBook Pro’s introduction. In January, South Korean blog Naver reported that Samsung had begun production on its new 8.6-generation OLED manufacturing line, which is expected to supply panels for the next-generation MacBook Pro, further supporting that timeframe. Gurman also reported in February that the redesigned MacBook Pro would arrive in the “back half” of 2026.
Gurman’s more recent reporting points to an October announcement and November availability. However, the launch was previously predicted for early 2027. In April, Gurman reported that supply-chain constraints were affecting development of the redesigned MacBook Pro and could push the release into early 2027. He subsequently reported in June that Apple had revised its chip roadmap, with the touchscreen MacBook Pro now expected to launch with M5 Pro and M5 Max chips instead of M6 Pro and M6 Max in an effort to keep the project on schedule. 


						

							


Which MacBook models will get a touchscreen? 
Current rumours suggest that Apple’s first touchscreen laptop will be a redesigned MacBook Pro with Pro and Max chips
Both Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman and analyst Ming-Chi Kuo have reported that Apple is developing MacBook Pro models with OLED touchscreen displays as part of a major redesign. The feature is expected to debut on the high-end MacBook Pro models powered by Apple’s Pro and Max chips, making them the first Macs to support direct touch input.
Apple is expected to use the touchscreen as a key differentiator for its professional laptops, further separating the MacBook Pro from the more affordable MacBook Air and MacBook Neo.
There is also speculation that Apple could rebrand the flagship model as the MacBook Ultra. According to one report from a source said to be familiar with Apple’s plans, the company intends to expand its “Ultra” branding beyond the Mac Studio and Apple silicon chips. However, this claim has not been corroborated by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman or analyst Ming-Chi Kuo, so it should be treated with caution.
For now, the technology appears set to remain exclusive to the MacBook Pro lineup. Neither the MacBook Air nor the MacBook Neo is expected to gain touchscreen support in the near term. However, Kuo believes Apple could eventually expand the technology to other MacBook models if the touchscreen MacBook Pro proves successful.
The MacBook Air may be the next candidate for a touchscreen upgrade, but current forecasts suggest this is unlikely before 2028 or 2029. Some reports also indicate that the Air could adopt OLED display technology before then, albeit without touch functionality.


						

							


Touchscreen MacBook Pro Design
Lighter design expected
Punch hole for the FaceTime camera
Apple’s touchscreen MacBook Pro is expected to have a substantially lighter design than current models, but it may not be significantly thinner. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman has revised his earlier expectations for a slimmer body while maintaining that Apple has redesigned and consolidated internal components to reduce weight. 
One of the most significant visual changes could be the removal of the display notch. Reports from display analysts and Bloomberg suggest Apple may replace the current notch with a hole-punch camera cutout, allowing for more usable screen space around the sensor. In early 2026, Gurman went a step further, claiming the new MacBook Pro could adopt an iPhone-like Dynamic Island interface built around the camera cutout.
The touchscreen MacBook Pro is also expected to retain its traditional laptop design, complete with a full keyboard and large trackpad, rather than becoming a hybrid tablet device.
Other rumoured design changes include:
A lighter chassis, although the latest reporting suggests it may not be thinner.
OLED display technology.
A hole-punch FaceTime camera replacing the notch.
Possible Dynamic Island-style functionality.
A reinforced hinge designed to minimise screen movement when the display is touched.
These changes would help distinguish the MacBook Pro from the MacBook Air and the entry-level MacBook Neo while giving Apple’s flagship laptop its most substantial design update in years.


						

							


Which chip will feature in the touchscreen MacBook?
M5 Pro and M5 Max
Early rumors suggested that Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook Pro would feature M6 Pro and M6 Max chips, but more recent reports indicate that Apple has changed its plans. The redesigned OLED models are now expected to launch with M5 Pro and M5 Max processors, with Apple potentially skipping the M6 Pro and M6 Max generation entirely.
According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman in June 2026, Apple has revised its chip roadmap to accelerate development of the AI-focused M7 generation. The change could bring the M7 chips to market around six months earlier, with significantly improved on-device AI capabilities. The ongoing DRAM and NAND shortages may also have influenced Apple’s decision, although they are not thought to be the primary reason. Apple has already increased Mac and iPad prices in response to rising memory costs. Read more about Apple’s reported chip roadmap changes.
Separately, Apple is reportedly planning to update the entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro with an M6 chip on October 27, retaining the existing design. 
These newer reports supersede earlier claims that the touchscreen MacBook Pro would use M6-series processors built on TSMC’s 2nm process. Leaked Apple files discovered by MacRumors in late 2025 also appeared to reference M6 MacBook Pro models, suggesting Apple had been developing M6-based hardware before reportedly changing direction.
There has also been speculation that Apple could introduce its own 5G modem to a future MacBook Pro, enabling cellular connectivity without Wi-Fi or an iPhone hotspot. However, there is little concrete evidence that cellular connectivity will be part of the touchscreen redesign.


						

							


Touchscreen MacBook Display
Tandem OLED display
Touchscreen interface
The display is expected to be the headline upgrade of Apple’s redesigned MacBook Pro. Multiple reports suggest Apple will replace the current Liquid Retina XDR (mini-LED) panel with a touchscreen OLED display, bringing MacBook Pro technology closer to the Ultra Retina XDR display used in the latest iPad Pro.
According to analyst Ming-Chi Kuo, Apple is planning to introduce OLED touch panels in the MacBook Pro in late 2026 or early 2027. The new display is expected to be thinner, more power-efficient, and capable of delivering deeper blacks, higher contrast, richer colours, and improved HDR performance than today’s mini-LED screens.
Reports indicate that both the 14-inch and 16-inch models will use advanced tandem OLED technology, which combines two OLED layers to achieve higher brightness levels while maintaining excellent energy efficiency. Apple first introduced this technology with the M4 iPad Pro and is expected to bring a similar implementation to the MacBook Pro.
The touchscreen functionality will reportedly rely on on-cell touch technology, which integrates touch sensors directly into the display rather than adding a separate layer. This approach helps keep the panel thin while supporting multi-touch input.
If the rumours prove accurate, the move to a tandem OLED touchscreen would represent the biggest display upgrade in the MacBook Pro’s history and one of the most significant changes to the lineup in years.

				
					

				
			The iPad Pro has a tandem OLED display, the type of display that could make its way into the 2026 MacBook Pro.
Brady Snyder / Foundry



							


Touchscreen MacBook Interface 

				
					

				
			macOS 27 could have some hidden touchscreen features. 

Foundry




Apple is not expected to turn macOS into iPadOS, but reports suggest macOS 27 could include subtle design changes to make the Mac easier to use with touch input.
Rather than replacing the traditional desktop experience, Apple is reportedly working on a touch-tuned interface that adapts depending on how the device is being used. When touch input is detected, interface elements such as menus, buttons, and controls may automatically enlarge to make them easier to tap. When using a mouse or trackpad, macOS would revert to its familiar point-and-click layout.
The touchscreen itself is expected to support standard gestures such as tapping, scrolling, and zooming, while still allowing users to switch between touch, trackpad, and mouse input.
Further clues appeared in the macOS 27.2 beta on October 5. MacRumors reported new code references to touch gestures in Safari, Photos, Notes and Quick Look. These could support a future touchscreen MacBook, but they could also relate to Sidecar, which allows an iPad to act as a Mac display. 
More specific clues appeared in footage shared by itspdfu on October 14. The footage reportedly shows touch-oriented behavior in Safari in macOS 27.2 betas 3 and 4: tabs lift and enlarge while being rearranged, then return to their normal size when dropped into place. Pressing and holding a tab opens a contextual menu that omits the Ask Siri option available with a mouse or trackpad. These changes suggest Apple is preparing Safari for touch input.


						

							


Touchscreen MacBook Pro: Connectivity 
5G connectivity could finally come to the Mac

				
					

				
			The C1X is now available, but the C2 modem could arrive with the 2026 MacBook Pro.
Apple




Beyond the touchscreen display and redesigned chassis, one of the most intriguing rumours surrounding the next-generation MacBook Pro is built-in cellular connectivity.
Apple has spent the past several years developing its own modem technology, beginning with the C-series modem family. Reports suggest the company has explored bringing 5G connectivity to the MacBook lineup, allowing users to connect directly to mobile networks without relying on Wi-Fi or a smartphone hotspot.
In August 2025, Macworld reported that internal Apple code referenced a MacBook Pro with an M5 Pro chip and Apple’s C1 modem. This suggests Apple has experimented with cellular-equipped MacBooks, althogugh it does not establish that the upcoming touchscreen models will offer 5G.
The redesigned MacBook Pro could also benefit from Apple’s growing portfolio of wireless chips. The company’s N-series networking processors, which handle Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and Thread connectivity, may eventually replace third-party components throughout the Mac lineup. An updated version of the chip could debut alongside the touchscreen MacBook Pro, improving power efficiency and tighter integration with Apple’s ecosystem.


						

							


Touchscreen MacBook Pro: Price expectations
Apple will likely offer similar configurations to the current MacBook Pro models, but it’s unclear how much of a premium a touchscreen OLED display will command. Apple upped the price of the iPad Pro by $200 when it got a tandem OLED, so it’s likely the touchscreen MacBook Pro will have a higher starting price.
Here are the prices for the current standard configurations of the M5 MacBook Pro, which saw prices increase between $300 and $500 in June 2026.
14-inch MacBook Pro
$1,999/£1,999: M5 with a 10-core CPU, 10-core GPU, 16GB unified memory, 1TB SSD, Thunderbolt 4
$2,499/£2,499: M5 Pro with a 15-core CPU, 16-core GPU, 24GB unified memory, 1TB SSD, Thunderbolt 5
$4,099/£4,099: M5 Max with a 18-core CPU, 32-core GPU, 36GB unified memory, 2TB SSD, Thunderbolt 5
16-inch MacBook Pro
$2,999/£2,999: M5 Pro with a 18-core CPU and 20-core GPU, 24GB unified memory, 1TB SSD, Thunderbolt 5
$4,399/£4,399: M5 Max with a 18-core CPU, 32-core GPU, 36GB unified memory, 2TB SSD, Thunderbolt 5

title: M6 MacBook Pro: Everything we know about Apple’s next laptop
content:
Macworld





Apple is expected to launch a new 14-inch MacBook Pro with the standard M6 chip in October 2026. However, unlike previous generations, the M6 isn’t expected to be joined by more powerful M6 Pro and M6 Max versions.
Apple currently offers three processor options across the MacBook Pro range: the standard M5 in the entry-level 14-inch model, and the more powerful M5 Pro and M5 Max in the 14-inch and 16-inch models. The standard M6 is expected to replace the M5 almost exactly a year after its October 2025 launch.
According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple is preparing to announce the entry-level M6 MacBook Pro in late October, potentially ahead of its October 28 media event. The new model is expected to retain the existing design, with the faster processor providing the main upgrade.
The more substantial changes, including an OLED touchscreen and redesigned chassis, are reportedly reserved for premium MacBook Pro models that will continue to use M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. Rather than introducing M6 Pro and M6 Max processors, Apple is reportedly fast-tracking the M7 generation, with M7 Pro and M7 Max models expected in fall 2027. For more on the redesigned models arriving this year, see our touchscreen MacBook Pro guide.
That creates an unusual buying decision: choose the standard M6 MacBook Pro, opt for one of the redesigned touchscreen models with M5 Pro or M5 Max chips, or wait for the next generation of professional processors in 2027. Here’s what the latest reports suggest.


M6 MacBook Pro release date: When will it launch?
October 28, 2026 (confirmed media experience date)
On October 19, Apple announced a media event, dubbed “Pro and Tell” on October 28, 2026. This is expected to be the introduction of new Macs, including the M6 MacBook Pro.
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported on October 8 that Apple is planning to announce the M6 MacBook Pro on October 27, 2026. According to the report, the launch will include an online video presentation and an in-person component for the press.
More recently, reports have pointed to a media experience in Los Angeles on Wednesday, October 28, a day after Gurman’s originally reported announcement date. Apple could still unveil the new MacBook Pro on October 27 before giving invited journalists an opportunity to see the hardware the following day. 
Then on Monday October 19, Apple’s Greg Joswiak posted on X to say: “Can’t wait to pro and tell next week.”  Indicating that the MacBook Pro will be updated in the week of 26 October.  


Can’t wait to pro and tell next week. pic.twitter.com/3wUkxwq35i
— Greg Joswiak (@gregjoz) October 19, 2026





The M6 MacBook Pro is expected to launch alongside the first OLED touchscreen MacBook Pro, an M6 iMac, and an updated iPad mini. The new entry-level MacBook Pro is expected to retain its 14-inch display and existing design, with the M6 chip providing the main upgrade.
The late October announcement would fit Apple’s recent release pattern. The M5 MacBook Pro arrived in October 2025, while its predecessor launched in November 2024.
Of the five generations of MacBook Pro, five have been released in the October/November timeframe. The list below also demonstrates that Apple doesn’t always introduce the standard, Pro and Max versions of a chip generation together.  
M5 Pro & M5 Max MacBook Pro: March 2026
M5 MacBook Pro: October 2025
M4, M4 Pro & M4 Max MacBook Pro: November 2024
M3, M3 Pro & M3 Max MacBook Pro: November 2023
M2 Pro & M2 Max MacBook Pro: January 2023
M2 MacBook Pro: June 2022
M1 Pro & M1 Max MacBook Pro: October 2021
M1 MacBook Pro: November 2020
Following the October 27 or 28 announcement, Gurman has indicated that the new MacBook Pro will start shipping on November 6. Ongoing memory and storage chip shortages could still affect availability or delivery times. These supply constraints have already contributed to price increases across Apple’s Mac lineup.


						

							


M6 MacBook Pro: Chip details
Expected M6 specs:
Same 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU as in the existing M6 Mac mini
TSMC 2nm manufacturing process
Up to 170GB/s memory bandwidth
Improved AI processing with Neural Accelerators

				
					

				
			
The M6 chip is expected to incorporate new features for improved AI processing.

Apple




Apple has introduced the M6 chip in the Mac mini, giving us a clear idea of what to expect from the upcoming MacBook Pro. The M6 is Apple’s first M-series chip built using TSMC’s 2nm manufacturing process, bringing improvements to CPU, GPU, and AI performance.
The M6 in the Mac mini features a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU, up from the M5’s 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU. It also introduces Neural Accelerators in every GPU core and a dual 16-core Neural Engine, boosting performance in AI workloads. The M6 MacBook Pro is expected to benefit from the same architectural improvements, making it particularly appealing to users running AI-powered applications and local AI models.
The Mac mini also provides an indication of what to expect from memory bandwidth. Earlier rumors suggested the M6 could reach 200GB/s, but the M6 Mac mini delivers up to 170GB/s with 24GB or 32GB of unified memory. The 16GB configuration offers 153GB/s, matching the M5. This relatively modest increase could limit the performance gains delivered by the redesigned GPU.
Our analysis suggests that the additional GPU cores, higher clock speeds, and architectural improvements help the M6 deliver gains of 20 percent or more in 3D graphics performance. However, memory bandwidth limitations mean those gains aren’t as substantial as the additional processing power might suggest.
The MacBook Pro’s exact M6 specifications remain unconfirmed, but the Mac mini offers a useful preview of the chip’s capabilities. The key question is whether Apple will make further changes to the processor or memory configurations when it brings the M6 to the MacBook Pro.


						

							


M6 MacBook Pro: Other specifications and features
Existing 14-inch design expected; no OLED or touchscreen
The M6 MacBook Pro is expected to retain the existing 14-inch design, with few changes beyond the processor upgrade. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the display, chassis, and other hardware are likely to remain substantially unchanged from the M5 MacBook Pro.
That means buyers shouldn’t expect an OLED display or touchscreen on the standard M6 model. Those features are reportedly reserved for Apple’s redesigned premium MacBook Pro models, which are also expected to debut on October 27.

				
					

				
			
The M6 MacBook Pro could be the last entry-level model of this particular design.

Foundry




How is the M6 MacBook Pro different from the touchscreen MacBook Pro?
Apple is reportedly preparing two very different MacBook Pro updates for October 27.
The standard 14-inch MacBook Pro will move from the M5 to the M6 processor while retaining its familiar design. It should appeal to buyers who want the newer chip but don’t need a redesigned laptop.
The higher-end MacBook Pro models, meanwhile, are expected to introduce an OLED touchscreen, a reportedly thinner and lighter chassis, and potentially an iPhone-style Dynamic Island camera cutout. Despite these upgrades, the redesigned models will reportedly use M5 Pro and M5 Max chips rather than M6 Pro and M6 Max processors.
This reflects Apple’s reported decision to skip the M6 Pro and M6 Max generation and focus development resources on the M7 family, which is expected in 2027.
Although the standard M6 is a newer chip, the M5 Pro and M5 Max are designed for more demanding professional workloads, so buyers shouldn’t assume the M6 MacBook Pro will be the more powerful option. It’s a similar situation to the Mac mini lineup, where the standard model features the M6 chip while the higher-end configuration uses the M5 Pro. 
The choice could therefore come down to whether buyers prioritize the latest chip at a lower price or a more powerful MacBook Pro with a redesigned display and chassis.


						

							






FeatureM6 MacBook ProOLED touchscreen MacBook Pro

Expected announcementOctober 27, 2026October 27, 2026
ProcessorM6M5 Pro / M5 Max
Screen sizes14-inchPremium MacBook Pro sizes; expected 14- and 16-inch
DisplayExisting non-OLED displayOLED
TouchscreenNoYes
DesignExisting chassisThinner, lighter redesign
PriceFrom around $1,999Higher pricing expected

 






M6 MacBook Pro: Price
$1,999/£1,999 starting price possible
We haven’t heard any reports about the price of the entry-level M6 MacBook Pro, but we can look at recent price history to get an idea. When the M5 MacBook Pro was released in 2025, its starting price was $1,599. Apple bumped it to $1,699 when the M5 Pro and Max models arrived earlier this year and increased the starting storage to 1TB. This past June, however, Apple raised the price to $1,999 due to supply chain constraints. Those constraints aren’t going away anytime soon, and it’s likely that the higher price is now the new normal.
During Apple’s Q3 2026 financial announcement in July, Apple CEO Tim Cook and CFO Kevan Parekh made it a point to explain that the supply chain constraints will affect production costs for months to come. ” We expect the impact from supply constraints to increase significantly sequentially,” said Parekh. “The projected supply constraints in the September quarter affect iPhone, Mac, and iPad.” Cook said, “With less flexibility in supply chain, we expect the impact from the supply constraints to increase significantly sequentially.”
The existing M5 MacBook Pro starts at $1,999/£1,999, following the price increases introduced in June 2026, and the M6 could retain that starting price.
However, another price increase is possible. Ongoing memory and storage shortages continue to affect Apple’s manufacturing costs, and the company may need to pass some of those costs on to buyers.
The redesigned OLED touchscreen models are also expected to carry a premium over the existing MacBook Pro lineup, making the standard M6 a potentially more affordable alternative for buyers who want a new MacBook Pro without paying extra for the redesigned display and chassis.


						

							


Should you wait for the M6 MacBook Pro?
With Apple’s next MacBook Pro announcement reportedly just days away, there’s a strong argument for waiting before buying a new 14-inch MacBook Pro. 
Waiting until the end of October should provide a clearer picture of the M6 MacBook Pro’s performance, pricing, and availability, while potentially bringing discounts on the outgoing M5 model.
Wait for the M6 MacBook Pro if: You’re planning to buy the standard 14-inch MacBook Pro and don’t urgently need a new laptop. The M6 should provide improved CPU, GPU, and AI performance over the M5, without requiring a move to Apple’s more expensive Pro and Max models.
Consider the OLED touchscreen MacBook Pro if: You’re interested in a more substantial upgrade, particularly the rumored touchscreen display, OLED technology, and thinner design. Those models are expected to continue using M5 Pro and M5 Max processors, making them potentially better choices for demanding professional workloads.
Buy an M5 MacBook Pro now if: You need a laptop immediately or find a substantial discount. The existing M5, M5 Pro, and M5 Max MacBook Pro models remain capable machines, and a reduced price could make them better value than a newly launched M6 model.
Wait for the M7 MacBook Pro if: You’re particularly interested in OLED but don’t need the touchscreen. Reports suggest Apple’s entry-level MacBook Pro could adopt the redesigned OLED chassis in 2027 with an M7 processor, although the timing remains uncertain.
For most people considering the entry-level MacBook Pro, waiting until October 27 makes sense. Even if the M6 doesn’t offer enough of an improvement to justify its price, its arrival could create opportunities to buy the outgoing M5 model at a discount.

title: Next Apple event 2026: When is Apple’s next launch?
content:
Macworld





Apple announced HomeView, HomePod mini 2, a new Apple TV 4K and the Apple Home Collection at its “Welcome Home” launch on October 13, 2026. But that will not be its final announcements this month.
Apple has now indicated that new products are coming next week. On Monday October 19, Apple’s Greg Joswiak posted on X to say: “Can’t wait to pro and tell next week.” 
This follows news that Apple has invited selected media to another product launch experience, this time in Los Angeles on Wednesday October 28. That new date is a day after the date reported by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, who initially reported that another launch was planned for October 27. The product launch could still take place on the 27 October though.
Apple is expected to reveal a touchscreen MacBooks, an M6 14-inch MacBook Pro, an M6 iMac and an OLED iPad mini and these are likely to be the products being showcased at the media event. 
Apple typically has four main event windows each year: a spring event, WWDC in June, the iPhone event in September, and sometimes a further event in October. The company rarely confirms dates far in advance, and there’s no guarantee it will hold an event in every window. That leaves Apple fans – and anyone considering a new Apple device – wondering when the next event will happen and what might be announced. Fortunately, Apple’s annual schedule is fairly predictable, while reliable rumours often provide additional clues about what’s coming. That means we can make informed estimates about the timing of future keynotes and the products most likely to appear.Here’s everything we know about the next event Apple will hold – and beyond.


When is Apple’s next event?
October 28, 2026: Apple’s confirmed ‘Pro and Tell’ media experience in Los Angeles.
Apple has invited some media to a product launch experience on October 28 in Los Angeles. The event starts at 10 a.m. Pacific / 1 p.m. Eastern / 5 p.m. U.K. (clocks change on October 25 in the U.K.) 
The next launch may still take place on October 27, 2026, the date initially reported by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman.
Gurman previously said the launch will include a video presentation and a gathering for journalists. Apple held a “Welcome Home” experience for select media on October 13. In March, it also hosted an “Apple Experience” alongside three days of product announcements. Those launches suggest a possible model for late October.


						

							


What could Apple launch at the next event?
Apple is expected to unveil its long-rumored touchscreen MacBook Pro, a 14-inch MacBook Pro with an M6 chip, an M6 iMac and an OLED iPad mini at the reported October 27 or 28 launch.
Joswiak’s X post indicates that the MacBook Pro will be the headliner for the event: 


Can’t wait to pro and tell next week. pic.twitter.com/3wUkxwq35i
— Greg Joswiak (@gregjoz) October 19, 2026




							




Apple event calendar 2026: What has Apple launched this year?


TimescaleEvent themeDatesProducts

March Special Experience2-4 MarchLaunched: iPhone 17e, MacBooks Neo, Pro & Air, iPad Air
JuneWWDCJune 8Unveiled plans for: iOS, macOS, other software, AI and Siri
SeptemberiPhone eventSeptember 9Launched: iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, iPhone Duo, new Apple Watch, AirPods 5
OctoberWelcome Home Apple ExperienceOctober 13 Launched: HomeView, HomePod mini 2, new Apple TV, and Apple Home Collection
OctoberPro and Tell Media ExperienceOctober 28 confirmedRumored: touchscreen MacBook, M6 14-inch MacBook Pro, M6 iMac and OLED iPad mini
Spring 2027TBCTBCExpected: iPhone 18, iPhone 18e, iPhone Air 2

 



Apple has held four events so far in 2026, including its March and October hands-on Experiences. On March 4, the company invited select media to hands-on “experiences” in multiple locations. In the run-up to that date, Apple launched several products via press release, including the iPhone 17e, M4 iPad Air, and M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pro, M5 MacBook Air and the MacBook Neo.
The second event was WWDC, which began with a keynote on June 8. At the WWDC keynote Apple outlined the upcoming changes to its operating systems, including iOS 27 and macOS 27 Golden Gate.
In August Apple issued press releases to announce the new Mac mini and Mac Studio. 
At the September 9 event Apple unveiled the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, a foldable iPhone Duo, a new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and AirPods 5. 
Apple’s October 13 “Welcome Home” announcements included HomeView, a new smart-home display with a 7-inch touchscreen; HomePod mini 2; a fourth-generation Apple TV 4K with an updated Siri Remote; and the Apple Home Collection, a range of cameras, doorbells, locks, and thermostats developed with accessory partners.  

				
					

				
			
Calendars at the ready.

Foundry





 FAQ 


1.
How far in advance does Apple announce an event?
Apple usually announces its events around one to two weeks before they take place, although the timing varies. The October 13, 2026 Experience was announced just five days in advance. Apple also sometimes chooses to announce products via press release without holding an event. 





2.
What time will the next Apple Event start? 
The Pro and Tell media experience in Los Angeles will start at 10 a.m. Pacific. That’s 1 p.m. Eastern and 5 p.m. U.K. (the U.K. clocks change before this event.)
This won’t be a keynote in the traditional sense. 
Apple keynotes usually last between one and two hours and feature the CEO alongside various other Apple executives.
WWDC and the September event tend to be longer keynotes; the spring and late-fall events can be slightly shorter. 
For example, the September 2024 event was 1 hour 38 minutes.





3.
What time do Apple events normally start in U.S., U.K. and other global time zones?
Apple’s events tend to start at 10 am PT or 1 pm ET. That translates to the following times in the countries where most of our readers live:
U.S.: 10 am PDT, 11 am MDT, 12 pm CDT, 1 pm EDT
Canada: as above, plus 2 pm ADT
U.K.: 6 pm
Europe: 7 pm CEST, 8 pm EEST
India: 10:30 pm IST
Australia: next day — 1 am AWST, 2:30 am ACST, 3 am AEST
New Zealand: next day — 5 am NZST
The timings are generally the same for all Apple Keynotes, but can be slightly different if Apple holds the event during the period of a couple of weeks when the clocks have changed in the U.S. but not elsewhere (in 2026 the clocks will change in the U.S. on November 1, while in the U.K. they change on October 25).
Sometimes Apple holds events at different times, for example, in October 2023 the event was held in late afternoon in San Francisco, which meant it was midnight in the U.K. The event on October 13, 2026 started at 9 am in New York, 2 pm in the U.K.
If Apple doesn’t hold an event and instead just issues a press release, that usually happens around 8 am PT, 11 am ET and 4 pm U.K. time.





4.
How often does Apple hold events?
There can be as many as four Apple events in a year:  
Spring Event
WWDC in June
iPhone Event in September
Late Fall Event in October
This event calendar is by no means set in stone, though, with the spring and October events being less regular. Some years, Apple doesn’t hold a spring event at all. In 2025 Apple only held two events, preferring instead to announce new products via press release.





5.
Will there be a live stream at the next Apple Event?
There was no public livestream for the October 13 Experience and one isn’t expected for the rumored October 27 or 28 event.
Apple usually livestreams the iPhone announcement in September and the WWDC keynote in June. 





6.
Does Apple ever announce products without an event? 
Apple frequently announces products without a keynote event, often opting for press releases or multi-day announcement windows. In recent years, the company has increasingly reserved its large-scale media events for major flagship launches, such as the primary iPhone lineup in September, while using press releases for iterative updates or “chip bumps” that may not warrant a full hour-long presentation.





7.
How to watch an Apple event
Apple events are typically broadcast across several digital platforms, allowing viewers to tune in from almost any device. While the company previously restricted access to its own hardware or the Safari browser, these barriers have been removed in recent years.
You can access live Apple presentations through the following official channels:
YouTube: This is often considered the easiest way to watch. Apple streams its keynotes live on its official YouTube channel, which can be accessed via any web browser or the YouTube app on smartphones, tablets, and smart TVs.
Apple.com: The company hosts a dedicated “Events” page on its official website. For the best experience on a PC, it is recommended to use Microsoft Edge on Windows 10 or later.
Apple TV App: The stream is available within the Apple TV app on iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Apple TV hardware. Keynotes are usually listed in the app’s lineup a day or two before the event begins.
Apple Podcasts: Apple also showcases its events through the Podcasts app on Apple devices, where you can watch the video presentation.
We usually run a Live Blog which will provide minute-by-minute text updates and analysis as products are announced.
Following the end of the event, detailed breakdowns will also be available on the Macworld Podcast, which can be found on Spotify, Soundcloud, and Apple Podcasts. 








Will Apple have a second October event in 2026?

				
					

				
			
Apple




Apple has already unveiled new products on October 13 at an ‘Apple Experience’ in New York, but it seems there are more product launches in the pipeline.
A separate Mac and iPad launch is reportedly planned for October 27 or 28. A touchscreen MacBook, M6 14-inch MacBook Pro, M6 iMac and OLED iPad mini are rumored.


						

							


Will Apple hold a spring event in 2027? 

				
					

				
			John Ternus: Apple’s new CEO.
Michael Simon / Foundry




Apple’s spring events have become increasingly unpredictable. The company has not held a traditional spring event since May 2024, although it did invite members of the media, including Macworld, to a “Special Apple Experience” in 2026. 
Rather than a keynote presentation, the March 4, 2026 gathering was a hands-on showcase that followed three days of product announcements, including the MacBook Neo, iPhone 17e, and M5 MacBook Air.
Will Apple take a similar approach to spring product launches in 2027? It’s certainly possible. The format appeared to work well, allowing each product announcement to receive its own media coverage rather than competing for attention during a single event. 
Apple is expected to release three iPhone models in spring 2027 – or it could be two new iPhones, with the Air and iPhone 18 merging.
iPhone 18 (base model)
iPhone 18e
iPhone Air 2
Apple may also update the MacBook Air with an M6 processor in spring 2027. 


						

							


When is WWDC 2027?

				
					

				
			
Foundry




When is the WWDC keynote?
In 2026 the WWDC keynote was on Monday June 8. In 2025 it started on Monday June 9. We expect WWDC will start on Monday 7 June in 2027. 
WWDC generally runs from the Monday to Friday in the second week of June. 
What Apple could launch at WWDC
WWDC is Apple’s big developer event at which it reveals plans for the operating systems that run on Apple hardware.
In June 2027 we expect Apple to unveil details of iOS 28, iPadOS 28, macOS 28, updates to watchOS, tvOS, HomePod software, and an update to Apple’s realityOS.
Apple sometimes announces new hardware at WWDC, usually the high-end models targeted at power users, so we could see new Macs.
Following the keynote on Monday, developer events and sessions will run throughout the week. You can read more about WWDC date, times and everything you need to know in a separate article.


						

							


What did Apple launch at past events?
So far in 2026 Apple has held an ‘experience’, which rather than being an event in the traditional sense, was a chance for journalists to get a look at products Apple had launched in the days prior, including MacBook Neo and iPhone 17e. The company also hosted the WWDC keynote on June 8, at which it revealed its plans for Apple Intelligence and Siri in iOS 27, macOS 27 and the other operating systems. Apple held its iPhone launch event on September 9 at which the iPhone 18 Pro and Max, iPhone Duo, Apple Watch Series 12, Apple Watch Ultra 4 and AirPods 5 launched. Plus Apple has unveiled new Home focused products (HomeView, HomePod mini 2 and Apple TV 4K) at a “Welcome Home” experience on October 13. 
In 2025 Apple only held two events. The first was its Worldwide Developers Conference (WWDC) on June 9, at which it introduced the new features coming in the next version of its operating systems, and the second was the huge September 9 Apple Event where it launched new Apple Watches, new AirPods Pro and the new iPhones for 2025.
Apple doesn’t have to hold an event to launch new products though. Prior to WWDC, Apple launched a new iPhone 16e via press release on February 19, a new iPad and iPad Air via press release on March 4, and a new MacBook Air and Mac Studio on March 5. 
Apple then went on to launch a new M5 MacBook Pro and M5 iPad Pro in October. No event was held to mark these launches.
In 2024, Apple held three events: one on Tuesday, May 7, at which it launched new iPads; a keynote to kick off WWDC on June 10; and an event on September 9 at which Apple unveiled the new iPhone 16, Apple Watch Series 10 and the AirPods 4. In October 2024 there was no event, but Apple did announce new products (iMac, Mac mini and MacBook Pro) via press release.
In 2023 there were three events: WWDC in June, an iPhone event in September, and Apple’s second fall event on October 30 (or after midnight on October 31 if you weren’t in the U.S.).
In 2022 Apple held three events: a spring event on March 8, WWDC on June 6, and the iPhone 14 launch on September 7. In other years Apple has held four events though.

title: This MacBook Pro isn’t just cheap, it’s $400 less than Apple’s pre-surge price
content:
Macworld





		
Apple MacBook Pro M5 Max
View Deal
If you want the best laptop you can possibly get, you’d better be prepared to spend quite a bit of money. The RAM and storage crisis has forced Apple and the rest of the industry to raise prices on just about everything, with the highest-end laptops getting the biggest increases. For example, the top-of-the-line 16-inch M5 Max MacBook Pro with 36GB of RAM and 2TB of storage jumped $500, from $3,899 to $4,399, and we haven’t seen it dip much below $4,000 since. 
Until now. Amazon is selling this MacBook Pro for $3,499, a whopping savings of $900 off its current MSRP and $400 under the price it was before the Great Summer Price Hike. That’s not just a great deal; it’s the lowest price we’ve ever seen, before or after the price hike.
The best part is that this is really a pro-level laptop that can handle all your projects, whether you’re editing video or working on AI models. The device runs on the M5 Max chip with an 18-core CPU and a 32-core GPU that will make video edits and 3D work run as smoothly as butter. Each GPU core has a Neural Accelerator, so AI tools run right on the laptop too. With 36GB of unified memory, you can keep dozens of apps and tabs open without issue. The 2TB SSD holds plenty of files, too, and you’re unlikely to need an upgrade anytime soon.
The spacious 16.2-inch Liquid Retina XDR display is stunning, hitting 1600 nits peak brightness with an impressive contrast ratio. There are three Thunderbolt 5 ports that can handle fast drives and up to four external displays. You also get HDMI, an SD card slot, MagSafe charging, and Wi-Fi 7. In short, you won’t have to worry about upgrading for years.
So go grab it for $3,499 while it’s still $900 off because this deal won’t last forever. And we doubt it’ll go much lower, even with Black Friday around the corner.

Google Wallet and Samsung Wallet will also be supported, with a related Samsung press release mentioning availability in the U.S. and Canada.

GM's digital keys use ultra-wideband technology to enable secure, proximity-based authentication, along with Bluetooth. They work with the iPhone 11 or later (excluding iPhone SE 2, iPhone SE 3, and iPhone 16e) or an Apple Watch Series 6 or later.

title: ‘HomeView Ultra’ with robot arm may be coming next year
content:
Macworld





HomeView will probably sell just fine, partly because it’s a comparatively affordable $299 and partly because it has the excitement and cachet of a brand-new Apple product. But that doesn’t mean it’s flawless. After all, HomeView is a first-gen device, and such devices nearly always suffer from problems that will be addressed in later versions.
In the latest edition of his Power On newsletter, Bloomberg leaker Mark Gurman draws attention to what he thinks is an obvious shortcoming of the HomeView: its inability to turn its screen to face the user. “In one commercial,” he writes, “a family passes the unit around… Each person has to physically turn the screen toward themselves. It’s an awkward demonstration for a device that’s supposed to make interacting with technology in the home more seamless.” This unwitting demonstration of a failing with the product, Gurman argues, “practically screams for a display that can turn on its own.”
Fortunately Gurman has good news for anyone who is similarly disenchanted by the lack of an auto-swivelling screen on the first-gen HomeView. The next version of the product, he claims, will feature a motorised robotic arm which will enable the screen to turn through 360 degrees and (based on voice recognition software) automatically face whoever is talking to it. “Imagine a FaceTime call where the screen follows you as you move around the kitchen,” he explains, “or a family gathered around a countertop with the display automatically turning toward whoever is speaking.”
The new model, Gurman stresses, is not just a sequel: it’s an upgrade. Aside from the robotic arm it will also boast a larger screen, up from 7 inches to 9. It probably won’t just be called HomeView, with likely branding options including a Max or Ultra suffix.
This isn’t the first time we’ve heard about a robotic smart device. Last year, Apple published a paper describing research into the technology (with videos), and we’ve read rumors about such a device for years.
Gurman claims this version of HomeView is already in development and carries the codename J595. (The original HomeView is J490.) It’s planned for release in 2027 or 2028, he adds. That’s quite a large window, but the development cycle for the original device lasted so long, he says, that long-departed Apple employees popped up after its launch to boast of involvement in its creation. Hopefully we won’t have to wait quite so long this time around.

title: Apple Photos faceprint privacy lawsuit pared down a bit, will continue

Photos' facial features are at the heart of a privacy lawsuit

However, in a September 30 filing by U.S. District Judge Nancy Rosenstengel, the class-action fight has been severely cut back. In a 34-page filing, the judge partially agrees with an Apple motion, while decertifying one of the subclasses in the suit.

title: iPhone Duo Guide: Everything you need to know about Apple’s foldable iPhone
content:
Macworld





Apple’s first foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo, goes on sale on October 23, but buyers who missed the first wave of preorders face a much longer wait. Delivery estimates slipped rapidly after orders opened on October 16, with Macworld’s U.S. tracking showing January 25, 2027 within around half an hour. Apple continues to accept orders. Prices start at $1,999/£1,999.
The Duo opens like a book from a compact 5.4-inch phone into a much larger 7.6-inch device. Apple describes the internal screen as its largest-ever iPhone display, with 50 percent more screen area than the iPhone 18 Pro Max, while the outer display provides more than 90 percent of the screen area of an iPhone 18 Pro.
The biggest difference is obviously the folding design, but Apple has done more than simply add a hinge. The iPhone Duo will ship with iOS 27.1, which adapts to different positions and orientations with fold-specific interface and multitasking features. These include Split View, hands-free FaceTime and video, StandBy without charging, and layouts that move seamlessly between the two screens. Apple Pencil USB-C support is also coming later in 2026.
The other major changes are the 7.6-inch nano-texture inner display, Touch ID replacing Face ID, an A20 Pro processor with vapor-chamber cooling, and a dual-battery system designed around the two halves of the phone. Apple has also introduced camera features that exploit the second screen, including Duo Preview, Smart Take, Kid Cue and Duo FaceTime.
Much of the pre-launch reporting proved accurate: the Duo name, book-style design, roughly 7.7- and 5.4-inch screens, Touch ID, two 48MP rear cameras, two front-facing cameras, A20 Pro, C2 modem, MagSafe and the white/dark-blue colours were all anticipated.
iPhone Duo at a glance
Apple’s first folding iPhone, with 5.4-inch outer and 7.6-inch inner displays.
Touch ID replaces Face ID, with the fingerprint sensor incorporated into the side button.
A20 Pro with vapor-chamber cooling, including a new 2nm manufacturing process.
Dual-battery architecture, giving up to 44 hours of video playback on the outer display.
Fold-specific iOS and camera features, including Split View, Duo Preview, Smart Take, Kid Cue and hands-free use.
iPhone Duo: Top 10 features


Foldable designBook-style titanium design with precision hinge
Inner display7.6-inch Super Retina XDR OLED, 120Hz ProMotion
Outer display5.4-inch Super Retina XDR OLED, 120Hz ProMotion
ProcessorA20 Pro, 6-core CPU, 7-core GPU
Neural EngineDual 16-core Neural Engine
AuthenticationTouch ID in side button
Rear cameras48MP Main + 48MP Ultra Wide
BatteryDual batteries; up to 44 hours video on outer screen
ConnectivityC2 modem, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, second-gen UWB
Storage256GB, 512GB, 1TB or 2TB

 






iPhone Duo release date: When will it go on sale?
Apple unveiled the iPhone Duo on September 9, 2026, alongside the iPhone 18 Pro, but its first foldable iPhone won’t reach customers until October 23.
Preorders opened on Friday, October 16, at 5 a.m. Pacific / 8 a.m. Eastern / 1 p.m. BST. Customers can order through Apple’s website or the Apple Store app, choosing from Star White and Night Sky finishes and 256GB, 512GB, 1TB or 2TB of storage.
The October 23 launch covers more than 70 countries and regions, including the U.S. and U.K., with another 28 markets following on October 30. The Duo will also be available through Apple Stores, selected carriers and authorized retailers, although availability varies by market.
However, launch-day delivery allocations were exhausted quickly, and customers ordering now face a substantially longer wait.
Pre-order iPhone Duo at Apple U.S. 
Pre-order iPhone Duo at Apple U.K. 
$1999 at  Apple						
					


						

							


Has the iPhone Duo sold out? 
Initial delivery allocations sold out rapidly, but Apple is still accepting preorders. 
As of October 19, Apple was quoting January 22, 2027 for delivery of the 256GB iPhone Duo in the U.S. and January 25, 2027 in the U.K. Estimates can change and depend on the configuration and delivery location.
Apple described preorder demand as “nothing short of extraordinary” and said it was working to get devices to customers as quickly as possible.
Supply constraints may also contribute to the backlog. A late-September report claimed that Apple and its manufacturing partners were experiencing low production yields. Long delivery waits therefore reflect the balance between demand and available supply, rather than revealing how many phones Apple has sold.


						

							


iPhone Duo design: What does it look like?

				
					

				
			
The iPhone Duo opens up like a book.

Apple




The iPhone Duo uses a book-style folding design. Closed, it is unusually short and wide for an iPhone, measuring 84.1mm wide, 117.8mm tall and 11.3mm thick. Open it and the width expands to 164.6mm, while thickness reduces to just 5.2mm, making it Apple’s thinnest iPhone when unfolded (taking that mantle from the iPhone Air). It weighs 254g.
The outer screen measures 5.4 inches, while the folding inner panel measures 7.6 inches. Both are Super Retina XDR OLED displays with ProMotion up to 120Hz, Always-On display support and up to 3,000 nits outdoor peak brightness. The internal display also has a nano-texture surface designed to reduce reflections and make the crease less noticeable. The inner display also has a replaceable top cover layer. AppleCare+ lists replacement at $19, although it must be replaced by Apple rather than peeled off like a conventional screen protector. Apple has not yet published the price without AppleCare+.
The frame and hinge cover are made from Grade 5 titanium. Apple uses a mirror-polished finish on the enclosure and a micro-blasted finish on the 3D-printed hinge cover. Ceramic Shield protects the rear, while Ceramic Shield 2 protects the outer display. The phone retains an IP68 rating despite its folding construction.

				
					

				
			
The hinge from the outside.

Apple




There are just two colors: Star White and Night Sky, essentially confirming the pre-event reports of silver/white and a very dark blue. For more information read about the iPhone Duo colors.
Action button and Camera Control
There is Camera Control, giving access to exposure, depth, zoom, cameras, styles and tone. It can also launch the new Siri Camera mode.
However, Apple’s Duo doesn’t feature an Action button. The regular iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max retain both the Action button and Camera Control, so this is one hardware-control compromise of the folding model.
Accessories
Apple is also launching two dedicated accessories for the foldable: 
The iPhone Duo Case at $79/£79
The Duo Folio with Kickstand at $129/£129
Both became available to order on October 16.


						

							


Face ID, Touch ID and the notch
Perhaps the most surprising difference between the iPhone Duo and Apple’s other flagship iPhones is that there is no Face ID.
Instead, Apple has brought back Touch ID, with the fingerprint sensor incorporated into the side button. It works whether the Duo is folded or unfolded, and Apple Watch can also be used to unlock the device. This confirms one of the most persistent pre-launch rumors.
The internal display therefore does not need the TrueDepth sensors used for Face ID. Its FaceTime camera sits beneath the display and disappears when it isn’t being used, giving the inner screen a largely uninterrupted surface.
The inner camera itself is hidden below the display rather than sitting permanently in a visible camera cutout. And yet, despite this and the absence of Face ID, there is still support for Dynamic Island.


						

							




iPhone Duo cameras: What cameras does it have?

				
					

				
			
There are two cameras on the rear.

Apple




The Duo has a 48MP Dual Fusion camera system, comprising:


CameraResolutionEquivalent focal lengthAperture

Fusion Main48MP26mmf/1.6
2x crop from Main12MP52mmf/1.6
Fusion Ultra Wide48MP13mmf/2.2
Outer front camera12MP—f/2.2
Inner FaceTime cameraApple does not specify resolution—f/1.8

 



The Duo does not have variable aperture. Variable aperture is exclusive to the 48MP Fusion Main camera in the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.


The biggest camera features for iPhone Duo
Duo Preview
The outer screen can show a live preview while somebody else is being photographed, allowing the subject to adjust their pose and framing.
Smart Take and Kid Cue
Smart Take detects when everybody is ready and automatically captures the shot. Kid Cue uses animations on the outer screen to encourage children to look towards the camera.
Two-screen shooting
The folding design supports unusual shooting configurations, including using the main cameras for selfies or group photos while seeing the composition on the other screen. Duo FaceTime can also put nearby participants onto the outer display.
Other notable camera features include 48MP macro photography, a 2x optical-quality crop from the Main camera, an under-display inner FaceTime camera, Dual Capture for simultaneous front-and-rear video, and 4K Dolby Vision recording at up to 120fps.


						

							


Rear cameras
The 48MP Fusion Main has an f/1.6 aperture, sensor-shift stabilization and can shoot 24MP or 48MP images. It also provides a 12MP, 2x optical-quality crop equivalent to a 52mm lens.
The 48MP Fusion Ultra Wide has a 13mm-equivalent lens, f/2.2 aperture and 120-degree field of view. It also supports 48MP macro photography and is the same Ultra Wide camera used by the iPhone 18 Pro family.
That means the Duo does not match the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max camera system. Those phones add a dedicated 48MP Fusion Telephoto and variable aperture on the Main camera, making the Pro models much more flexible for photography despite costing substantially less.
Pre-event reports were divided between a Main + Telephoto and Main + Ultra Wide arrangement. Apple ultimately chose Main + Ultra Wide, confirming the earlier reports that a dedicated telephoto could be sacrificed to save space.
Front cameras
On the outside is a 12MP Center Stage camera with an f/2.2 aperture. It supports Center Stage, automatic portrait/landscape framing, Dual Capture, Photonic Engine, Deep Fusion, Smart HDR 5 and 4K Dolby Vision video at up to 60fps.
Inside is an under-display FaceTime camera with an f/1.8 aperture. Apple does not specify its megapixel resolution. It supports Center Stage for video calls and records at up to 1080p/60fps. Its major advantage is visual rather than photographic: the camera effectively disappears beneath the display when it isn’t being used.
iPhone Duo video features
The Main camera records 4K Dolby Vision at 24, 25, 30, 60, 100 or 120fps, with 4K/120fps also available for slo-mo. Cinematic mode reaches 4K/60fps and Action mode up to 2.8K/60fps. Dual Capture can record at up to 4K/30fps.
Apple’s specifications also do not list ProRes or Apple Log recording for the Duo. Those remain more Pro-oriented capabilities rather than part of Apple’s foldable camera proposition.
The Duo does support Spatial Audio recording, Audio Mix, Dolby Vision HDR and Apple’s computational photography features including Photonic Engine, Deep Fusion, Smart HDR 5, Photographic Styles 3, smart focus tracking and Apple Intelligence-powered editing.
Apple does not list conventional Spatial Video capture in the Duo specifications.


						

							


iPhone Duo processor: What processor does it use?

				
					

				
			
Watch video on the screen.

Apple




The iPhone Duo uses the A20 Pro, the same processor as the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.
It is manufactured using a 2-nanometer process, a major step forward in transistor density and efficiency. Apple combines it with a new chip packaging design inspired by its M-series Mac processors. The package connects the A20 Pro directly to a custom vapor chamber to transfer heat away from the processor more effectively.
The A20 Pro includes:
6-core CPU: two super cores and four efficiency cores
7-core GPU with Neural Accelerators
Dual 16-core Neural Engine
Hardware-accelerated ray tracing
A dedicated display engine capable of operating both Duo displays
Compared with the A19 Pro, Apple says the CPU is up to 20 percent faster, while the GPU is up to 40 percent faster and more power-efficient. The Dual 16-core Neural Engine delivers twice the compute power, while unified-memory bandwidth rises by 50 percent.
Apple also claims that the complete thermal system gives the Duo up to 35 percent better sustained performance than the iPhone 17 Pro. That sustained-performance figure is particularly important for a folding device because prolonged gaming, multitasking and AI workloads generate considerably more heat than short benchmark bursts.


						

							


iPhone Duo RAM: How much memory does it have?
Apple has not disclosed how much RAM is inside the iPhone Duo.
Before launch, supply-chain reports consistently pointed to 12GB of RAM, which would make sense given the demands of running two displays, simultaneous applications, Siri AI and larger on-device AI models. 
Apple does reveal that A20 Pro has 50 percent more unified-memory bandwidth than A19 Pro, which should help the Duo move data more quickly between the CPU, GPU and Neural Engine.
Extra memory is particularly useful on the Duo because iOS 27.1 can display multiple apps simultaneously and because Apple Intelligence and Siri AI increasingly run generative models locally rather than relying entirely on cloud processing.


						

							


iPhone Duo connectivity

				
					

				
			
An expensive desk calendar. 

Apple




Apple has put a significant amount of its own communications silicon into the iPhone Duo.
It uses Apple’s new C2 cellular modem, replacing Qualcomm silicon. Apple says C2 introduces AI-powered improvements to cellular quality and reliability and supports mmWave 5G in the U.S.
The N1 wireless networking chip provides:
Wi-Fi 7 with 2×2 MIMO
Bluetooth 6
Thread networking
The USB-C port also supports USB 3 data transfers at up to 10Gbps and DisplayPort video output.
The Duo also has Apple’s second-generation Ultra Wideband chip, NFC and precision dual-frequency GPS.
It is eSIM-only worldwide, something that had been widely rumored before launch. Eliminating the SIM tray gives Apple additional internal space for its batteries.
iPhone Handoff – a feature introduced with iOS 27 – makes it easier to use an iPhone Duo alongside another iPhone without needing separate phone numbers. Both devices share your number, with calls, voicemail, messages and Find My location following whichever iPhone you unlock. Only one phone is active at a time. You could use the Duo’s folding display for work, then switch to an iPhone Pro when you want its telephoto camera. Both phones need iOS 27, eSIM support and the same Apple Account, with Messages in iCloud enabled. Your carrier must specifically support iPhone Handoff, and your plan may require an additional monthly fee for access. T-Mobile already offers iPhone Handoff for $5 a month; Verizon and EE (in the U.K.) plan support. Fees may apply.
Satellite capabilities include:
Emergency SOS via satellite
Roadside Assistance via satellite
Find My via satellite
Messages via satellite


						

							


Battery, MagSafe and charging: What’s available?
Instead of one battery spanning the body, the iPhone Duo contains two rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, with one high-energy battery fitted into each half of the device. Apple’s energy-balancing algorithms make them operate as a single battery system.
Apple rates battery life at:
Up to 24 hours of typical use
Up to 44 hours video playback using the outer display
Up to 31 hours using the inner display
Up to 37 hours streamed video on the outer screen
Up to 26 hours streamed video on the inner display
Apple has not disclosed the batteries’ combined capacity in mAh. The pre-launch rumor of approximately 5,000-5,500mAh therefore remains unconfirmed.
Apple says the iPhone Duo can reach 50 percent charge in around 20 minutes using a USB-C charging cable and a 60W-capable power adapter or higher.
MagSafe and Qi2 wireless charging are supported at up to 25W. Apple’s claimed 50 percent charge in around 30 minutes requires a MagSafe charger paired with a 35W-or-higher power adapter.
In both the U.S. and U.K., the box includes the iPhone Duo and a 1-meter USB-C charging cable, but no power adapter. The MagSafe charger is also sold separately, so factor these accessories into your budget if you don’t already own suitable equipment.


						

							




iPhone Duo price: How much does it cost?
The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 in the U.S. and £1,999 in the U.K. for 256GB.
Prices are:


StoragePrice

256GB$1,999/£1,999
512GB$2,199/£2,199
1TB$2,599/£2,599
2TB$3,199/£3,199

 



The 256GB starting capacity means Apple has not created an unusually low-storage entry model simply to make the headline price look lower.


iPhone Duo vs iPhone 18 Pro pricing
The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199/£1,199, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299/£1,299. That makes the Duo approximately $700/£700 more expensive than the Pro Max at entry level.
That premium buys the folding display, precision hinge, titanium structure, second screen and more complex dual-battery design rather than superior cameras: in several areas the iPhone 18 Pro models are actually better equipped.
Reports before the launch suggested the Duo could cost anywhere from around $1,999 to $2,399 at entry level, largely because of the folding OLED display, hinge mechanism, titanium components and other expensive parts. Apple ultimately landed at the very bottom of those predictions.


						

							


iPhone Duo software: Multitasking and Apple Pencil support
The iPhone Duo’s larger inner display enables Split View, letting you use two apps side by side. For example, you could keep Safari open while taking notes, or check your calendar alongside a conversation in Messages. Supported apps can also open two windows of their own: Safari can display two webpages side by side for comparison shopping. You can save pairs of apps to return to later.
StandBy also works differently on the Duo. Set the phone down and it can display a clock, photos or widgets on either screen without being connected to a charger. New Calendar and Weather faces join the existing options.
Apple Pencil support is coming later in 2026. Apple has announced compatibility with the Apple Pencil (USB-C), allowing users to write, sketch and mark up documents on either display. 


						

							


Should you buy the iPhone Duo?
The iPhone Duo is the iPhone to buy if you genuinely want a phone and small tablet in one device. Its 7.6-inch display, multitasking features, A20 Pro performance and clever fold-specific camera modes offer capabilities no other iPhone has. 
But at $1,999/£1,999 it is enormously expensive, and there are significant compromises: no Face ID, no dedicated telephoto camera, no variable aperture and no Action button. 
For photography, battery life and conventional everyday use, the iPhone 18 Pro Max is likely to be the better-value flagship. Buy the Duo because you want the folding experience, not because it is simply the “best” iPhone.

title: I want a HomeView. I just need a reason to buy one
content:
Macworld





Apple is very good at first impressions. The MacBook Air emerging from the manila envelope; the iPhone in Steve Jobs’ pocket; the first Macintosh saying “Hello.” Apple knows instinctively how to communicate in an instant what a product stands for, and why you should be excited about it. Which makes it all the more mystifying that senior management decided not to hold a live-streamed event to hype up the HomeView and other new home products last week.
If you ask me, in fact, Apple did a decent hype job even without the benefit of a full-dress keynote presentation. Not on the HomePod mini 2 and new Apple TV–the former is virtually an auto-buy and the latter an auto-ignore at that price–but on the HomeView. A simple press release and a few animations on the website have ensured that I really, really want one. Even though the rational part of my brain keeps pointing out that I don’t need one even slightly.
I covered this ground ahead of the launch, in a column where I said the main question would be, “What is it for?” I hoped that the launch would see Apple succeed in explaining the purpose of its latest foray into the smart home, or rather how that purpose is relevant to a mainstream audience. Maybe a full event would have given the company more space to explore the broader societal changes which it thinks will make the HomeView relevant to the average U.S. homeowner, but I suspect the unavoidable truth is that this simply isn’t a product with broad appeal.
What can you do with a HomeView? You can monitor and control a smart home, of course, but I suspect that Apple knows this is a niche concern; the clue is how far down the press release you have to go before you reach any mention of smart lights, locks, and thermostats (the 17th paragraph, by my count). In the future it’s plausible that we will all have HomeKit-compatible smart homes, but for now most people don’t. And those who do tend to control them with their phones, while using a HomePod or Apple TV as the hub.
While Apple waits for the world to catch up with the smart-home revolution–a process which will be accelerated by the launch of the HomeView, but still needs time–it has to fall back on its other functions. You can FaceTime and read recipes, talk to Siri AI, or play music with onscreen lyrics. You can use it as electronic photo frame, or an alarm clock. With the exception of superior audio you’re essentially getting an iPad which is locked in one place, has a smaller screen, and can’t install third-party apps.
The HomeView is not an iPhone, the sort of chameleonic device that will take over the world by being relevant and useful to virtually everyone. It’s not even an iPad, less portable and caught in the middle ground between phone and laptop, but nevertheless deeply versatile. Unlike those two products the HomeView is a specialist: a product capable of delivering one specific experience for a handful of purposes. And in that sense it’s closer to the first iteration of the Apple Watch or even, I’m sorry to say, the Vision Pro. It’s a luxury; a want-to-have rather than a must-have.
The HomeView’s saving grace is that at $299 it’s relatively affordable for a luxury. That’s significantly cheaper than the cheapest iPad, a product which customers have historically been willing to buy for non-essential use. (Although I suspect they were a lot more willing when it was closer to the HomeView’s price earlier this year.) It’s significantly cheaper than an Apple Watch Series 12, and not much more expensive than an Apple Watch SE.
You can scarcely call the HomeView a bargain or an impulse purchase, but this is a price point where customers are willing to be persuaded. And when it’s a completely new Apple product, and you can throw in the hype factor of that seductive first impression, you can bet it will sell just fine.

title: iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max colors: All the options explained
content:
Macworld





Apple’s new iPhones for 2026 are packed with impressive technology, from faster chips and upgraded cameras to sophisticated displays and new AI features. But choosing a new iPhone isn’t always just about what’s on the inside. Much like buying a car, for some people the colour is almost as important as the specifications. After all, if you’re going to carry something around with you every day for the next few years, you’ll probably want to like the way it looks.
Here’s what you need to know about the color choices available with the new iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone Duo.
You can also read about how we were able to leak the new colour options ahead of the event earlier this year. We described the standout iPhone 18 Pro shade as Dark Cherry, although Apple ultimately went with the less cheery name Burgundy. (We prefer our name for the shade.)


iPhone 18 Pro and Pro MaxBlack, Glacier, Burgundy and Silver
iPhone DuoStar White and Night Sky
iPhone 17 Pro & Pro MaxCosmic Orange, Deep Blue and Silver

 



iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max colors
The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max come in four finishes: Black, Glacier, Burgundy and Silver.

				
					

				
			iPhone 18 Pro in Burgundy.
David Price / Foundry




The most distinctive new option is Burgundy, a dark red wine shade that was variously described in pre-launch leaks as Dark Cherry, Dark Red, coffee brown and even purple. Those rumours proved remarkably accurate, even if the name didn’t.

				
					

				
			iPhone 18 Pro in Glacier (aka Light Blue).

Roman Loyola / Foundry




Anyone who missed having a dark Pro iPhone will welcome the return of Black, after Apple dropped a conventional black finish from the iPhone 17 Pro lineup. Silver also returns, while Glacier (a pale, icy blue) replaces last year’s much darker Deep Blue as the cooler, more colourful option.
Which iPhone 18 Pro color should you choose?
Apple offers four finishes for the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, but which one should you pick? Here’s what our reviewers thought of the new colors, along with our recommendations.


Burgundy – Best for making a statement
In our iPhone 18 Pro review, Jason Cross described Burgundy as a perfectly acceptable color, but disappointing compared with last year’s vibrant Cosmic Orange. Our sister publication, Tech Advisor, also found the new color palette more tasteful than exciting.
Our recommendation: Burgundy is the best choice if you want a distinctive iPhone that stands out without being quite as bold or bright as Cosmic Orange.
 


							


Silver – Best all-round choice
In its iPhone 18 Pro review, our sister publication Tech Advisor tested the Silver model and praised its matte finish. Reviewer Emma Rowley noted that the improved color matching between the glass back and aluminum frame makes the phone look smarter than its predecessor. She also found that the finish resisted fingerprints well.
Our recommendation: Silver is an excellent choice for anyone who values understated looks and everyday practicality. It’s arguably the safest all-round option.


						

							


Glacier – Best subtle alternative
Our reviewer Jason Cross found the Glacier finish considerably more subdued than last year’s brighter Pro models. Tech Advisor’s Emma Rowley described it as an icy blue.
Our recommendation: Glacier is a good choice if you want a little color without Burgundy’s stronger visual impact. Its pale blue finish offers something different from the more traditional Silver and Black. 


						

							


Black – Best traditional finish
Black returns to the Pro lineup after being absent from the iPhone 17 Pro range. It’s the most conventional of the four finishes, and neither of our reviewers offered a detailed assessment of its appearance or practicality.
Our recommendation: Black is the obvious choice for anyone who prefers a classic, understated dark iPhone. It won’t make the same statement as Burgundy, but that’s precisely its appeal.


						

							




iPhone Duo colors

				
					

				
			
It’s black or white. 

Apple




Apple’s first foldable iPhone has a much more restrained palette, with just two finishes: Star White and Night Sky. In simple terms, you’re essentially choosing between white and a very dark blue.
The understated colours complement the Duo’s polished Grade 5 titanium frame, helping give both versions a premium, jewellery-like appearance that distinguishes the foldable from Apple’s regular aluminium iPhones.
The limited selection isn’t a surprise. Reports had suggested for months that Apple’s first foldable would launch in just two colours, with white and dark blue eventually emerging as the leading possibilities ahead of the event.
What we discovered about the new colors before the launch…
Editor’s note: The following section preserves Macworld’s exclusive reporting from before Apple’s September 2026 launch. It reflects the information available to our sources at the time, including early color names, renders and development details. Apple subsequently confirmed the final finishes described above.
As in 2025, Macworld received information from a source familiar with Apple’s supply chain regarding the color options for the iPhone 18 lineup before the launch. We also had our own renders to show what to expect. Here’s what we discovered.
Dark Cherry
Every year, Apple introduces a new signature color for the iPhone Pro models. With the iPhone 17 Pro, the color that stood out the most was the vibrant Cosmic Orange. What about this year’s models?
While other sources have previously reported on a “Dark Red” color, the information we’ve heard suggests that Apple has been working on a Dark Cherry option (which we now know is called Burgundy) to serve as the headline new color for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. Previously, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman and other leakers had suggested that Apple has been experimenting with a shade of red for this year’s phones, but we can reveal the hue will be much closer to wine than fruit punch.
While the Dark Cherry color isn’t as bright and striking as Cosmic Orange in person, it will still be unique enough to distinguish it as the new iPhone 18 Pro. As always, Apple is expected to discontinue the current lineup of colors, including Cosmic Orange.

				
					

				
			
The iPhone 18 Pro could come in three all-new colors.

Foundry




Apple has also been reportedly experimenting with two other new color options for this year’s Pro lineup. One of them is Light Blue (which Apple calls Glacier), which would resemble the current Mist Blue color of the base iPhone 17. The other color in development is a dark shade of gray. Finally, our source also reports on the existence of a silver variant of the iPhone 18 Pro, similar to the current generation.
Once again, our source notes that the colors are all in development, but since the iPhone 18 Pro hasn’t gone into mass production yet, Apple still has time to change them. Also, bear in mind that Apple doesn’t always offer four color options for the Pro models, so one of these hues could be dropped.
Last year, both Macworld and the reliable leaker Sonny Dickson reported that Apple had also considered launching the iPhone 17 Pro in black or steel gray. However, those color options never saw the light of day. 
Here are the Pantone color codes our source says are being used internally by Apple:
Light Blue (Pantone 2121)
Dark Cherry (Pantone 6076)
Dark Gray (Pantone 426C)
Silver (Pantone 427C)
We used these codes to generate the image above. Of course, colors may look a bit different in real life due to the material and lighting conditions. Since this report was published, we’ve seen real-world evidence of these colors, specifically the Dark Cherry hue.
A very familiar design with minor changes
Macworld’s sources also had access to the CAD drawings of the new iPhones. These documents support the rumors that the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max will look very similar to their predecessors, with only minor changes.
Most notably, the renders show a smaller Dynamic Island on the screen, which has been rumored to be one of the changes for this year’s models. This means the display will have more screen space for content when the Dynamic Island isn’t showing Live Activities.

				
					

				
			
The Dynamic Island could be smaller on the iPhone 18 Pro.

Foundry




Another interesting change noted by our source is that, in one of the renders, the gap between the glass cutout on the back and the camera bump is a bit smaller. Our source was unable to verify whether this is an old render, or if Apple is moving forward with a design change.
Last year, a Weibo leaker known as Instant Digital reported that Apple would adopt a new process to minimize the color difference between the glass and the aluminum frame, so perhaps that change also involves reducing the gap between the glass and the camera bump at some point.
More neutral colors for the foldable iPhone
We’ve also received details about the color options for the rumored foldable iPhone. The device, which will reportedly look like an iPad mini when unfolded, won’t come in fun colors like the base iPhone and may have even fewer options than the iPhone Pro.
For the foldable iPhone, Apple has been working on a classic silver and white model, as well as an Indigo option similar to the iPhone 17 Pro’s Deep Blue.

				
					

				
			
The iPhone Fold will reportedly come in a dark Indigo option.

Foundry




The source also corroborates leaked CADs and renders showing the potential design of the foldable iPhone, which is expected to feature two rear cameras, a selfie camera on the outer display, and another selfie camera in the upper-left corner of the inner display. The schematics seen by our source reveal that the foldable iPhone will be just 4.7 millimeters thick when unfolded, making it significantly thinner than the 5.6mm iPhone Air.
The iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and the foldable iPhone are all expected to launch in September, while our sources also report that the foldable model will hit stores at a later date. The base model of the iPhone 18, the iPhone 18e, and a new Air have been rumored to arrive in the first half of 2027, which has also been confirmed by our source.

title: Mark Gurman: Apple Made 'Major Mistake' With iPhone Duo Pre-Orders
content:
